extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and learned men seeking guidance on methods of discovery and advancement of the sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance and diagnostic signs for conducting and improving natural philosophy (scientific inquiry), including correct ends, methods of experiment, institutional impediments, and intellectual pitfalls to avoid. Emphasis on moving from the senses to understanding via regulated experiment and on preparing minds to attempt invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not declare the unknown impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid considering everything which has been either unknown or unattempted by themselves or their teachers, as beyond the limits of possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon criticizes philosophers who, from the defects of their own discoveries, 'convert the defects of their own discoveries into a calumny on nature and a source of despair to every one else.' Such declarations deter inquiry and are rooted in pride and envy rather than evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimity is a poor test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: True unanimity requires free judgment after investigation; mere widespread assent often derives from prejudice and authority, not demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that unanimity in intellectual matters is usually obsequious concurrence rather than genuine agreement, and is often an unfavorable sign—nothing pleases the multitude unless it strikes the imagination or binds the understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for historical limits when judging progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that only a few epochs have been fertile to the sciences; the small proportion of ages favorable to scientific progress explains much of past stagnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Out of many centuries, Bacon notes scarcely six are 'fertile in science,' so assessing scientific development requires attention to historical contingencies and pauses (deserts and wastes) in learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore natural philosophy as the root of other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy (the study of nature) must be the source and nourishment of particular sciences; when separated, those sciences 'have no depth' and only 'glide over the surface.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon argues that astronomy, optics, music, medicine, moral and political philosophy, and logical sciences lack depth when cut off from contemplation of motion, rays, sounds, texture, conformation, and the affections of the understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow dedicated practitioners to pursue natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy seldom had exclusive practitioners free from other pursuits; progress requires individuals who devote themselves singularly to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless natural philosophy gains exclusive possession of some investigators (not merely as a 'handmaid' to other arts), significant advances cannot be expected; partial or incidental attention yields limited growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix the proper end of science: useful inventions and benefits to life
rubrics_metrics.description: The legitimate goal of the sciences is 'the endowment of human life with new inventions and riches', not merely speculative satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many teachers fail to pursue this end, preferring reputation or contemplation. Bacon insists that setting this practical goal would direct inquiry toward productive investigations and real effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a regulated method from senses to understanding via experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The correct order begins with the senses and regular, well-conducted experiment: 'set up a light, and then show the road by it, commencing with a regulated and digested...course of experiment, and thence deducing axioms, and from those axioms new experiments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with the common 'loose fagot' of chance experience or vague groping—Bacon prescribes methodical experiments leading to axioms, not chaotic trial-and-error or premature theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on logic or mere opinion for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic and the practice of collecting others' opinions plus one's reflections do not truly discover first axioms or principles; such methods are 'without foundation' and 'merely turn on opinion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic discovers what accords with given axioms but does not produce the foundational principles themselves; therefore discovery must rely on regulated empirical methods rather than purely dialectical exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the contempt for experiment as degrading to intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceit that the dignity of the human mind is lowered by intercourse with experiments (matters of sense) is vainglorious and prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon condemns dismissal of experimental labor as 'mean' or 'unproductive'; such disdain has led to the neglect and interception of the true path to knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not revere antiquity or authority to the detriment of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration for antiquity and infinite credit to particular authors retards advancement; truth is 'the daughter of time, not of authority.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should expect more mature judgment from one's own age, since the world's accumulated observations increase; blind deference to writers of the past enchains the power of man from confronting things themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware admiration of polished effects as evidence of deep knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration for perfected mechanical arts and liberal arts (clocks, manufacture, cuisine, etc.) leads to overestimating present wealth of knowledge while masking a poverty of underlying observations and axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many polished arts depend on few axioms and patient manual skill; mistaking refinement and craft for deep scientific understanding fosters complacency and hinders the pursuit of foundational discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize methods and divisions that mask emptiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems and divisions of sciences can present the form of a perfect science while being 'badly filled up'—appearance of completeness may be an 'empty bladder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier investigators used aphorisms and scattered sentences honestly; modern pretence of comprehensive systems often discourages further inquiry by suggesting that nothing more is to be sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate genuine new science from the taint of impostors
rubrics_metrics.description: The absurdity and levity of charlatans (promising transmutation, prolongation of life, divination, etc.) have prejudiced the public against legitimate new propositions, especially those claiming effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon advises that the excesses of impostors should not cause rejection of valid new endeavors; evaluate claims by evidence rather than by association with past imposture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let failures of current art be taken as proofs of natural impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners often convert the weakness of their art into a calumny upon nature, pronouncing what their art cannot do as physically impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is circular and self-defeating—art acting as judge in its own cause narrows human expectation and cuts off chances of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate hidden natures by studying their manifestations elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: It is poor practice to study a nature 'in itself alone'; phenomena that seem secret in one subject may be manifest in another and thus easier to research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon gives examples (consistency in wood vs thin pellicles of water); look for related, more tractable instances to reveal the hidden principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and counteract superstition and religious opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition and imprudent zeal for religion have opposed natural philosophy; some fear that inquiry may impinge upon sacred mysteries or weaken faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon argues natural philosophy, 'after the Word of God', is the surest remedy against superstition and the most approved support of faith—science should be framed as supporting, not undermining, religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform institutional instruction that chains minds to authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools, universities, and similar assemblies often oppose progress because lectures and exercises are ordered so that 'anything out of the common track can scarcely enter the thoughts' of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such institutions chain pursuits to writings of particular authors, and dissenters are labeled turbulent; reform is needed so that departments 'resound...with new works and advances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Align rewards and patronage with advancement of science
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultivation of science and its rewards historically do not fall to the same individual; lack of reward and popular praise represses scientific industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon notes that advancement is the work of powerful geniuses while prizes go to vulgar or poorly-informed patrons; to encourage progress, reward structures should value genuine scientific breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat despair and prepare minds with reasoned hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Men's despair and belief in the impossibility of further progress are a major obstacle; preparing minds with plausible reasons for success is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon recommends disclosing reasons for hope (as Columbus did for new lands) and showing that small beginnings and gradual providential increases ('the kingdom of God cometh without observation') lead to great advances; this psychological preparation is important for motivating experimenters.
